rv.q: The Addams Family is a thoroughly professional piece of commercial Broadway craftsmanship that does exactly what it sets out to do
And a lucky thing, too, since it is Lane and Hoffman’s ace comic timing, as well as the astringent poise of Bebe Neuwirth, as the mother Morticia, that keep things palatable.
But for those in love with Addams' dry sensibility, the trade-offs in banality may not be tolerable.
Indeed, only a handful of theatergoers are likely to find The Addams Family worth a second visit.
But “Addams Family” nonetheless seems an opportunity missed, lacking the comic inspiration that would have made it more than just a family alternative to “Wicked.”
It's definitely a feat of some kind: Broadway's "The Addams Family" has watered down one of the quirkiest pop- culture creations ever.
But $16.5 million has brought forth an ill-formed one-dimensional cartoon with lines and shading not quite inked in.
Addams’s poisoned brew is turned into Kool-Aid.
Being in this genuinely ghastly musical must feel like going to a Halloween party in a strait-jacket.

Oh Broadway, Broadway, Broadway. Don't you know, you never seem sadder or more imaginatively barren than when you're diving for commercial relevance in the dumpsters behind old TV shows and movies? 'The Addams Family' -- this year's answer to the question, How many talented people does it take to screw up a concept? -- marks a significant depres...
If you have a high tolerance for corn on the macabre, this is the show for you.
Besides being unoriginal it's uncompelling to boot.
The jokes, however artfully executed, are seldom surprising, and making cartoon characters who worked in the context of a half-hour sitcom compelling over 2 hours proves a serious stretch.
Even Nathan Lane's resourcefulness, Kevin Chamberlin's moonstruck charm, and Carolee Carmello's giddy vocal display can't reanimate this inert monstrosity.

'The Addams Family' is a musical all dressed up with no place to go. There's one simple reason: Nobody knew why they were writing it. There is no animating purpose to the evening, except to throw well-known characters on stage so the audience can luxuriate in their comforting familiarity.

If you want to know why musical comedy is such a difficult art form to master, a prime example is now on display at Broadway’s Lunt-Fontanne Theatre where "The Addams Family" has fitfully burst into story and song.

cn.t: Mixed reviews for this musical adaptation, with critics praising Nathan Lane and Bebe Neuwirth's performances but faulting a thin plot that strips away the source material's subversive edge.

sg.ra: Per SeatPlan and Headout, center rows D-J are the Lunt-Fontanne sweet spot because the house stage sits unusually high and is not raked — patrons halfway back in orchestra report they cannot see the stage floor, so anchoring forward of the overhang line (row W) but back from rows A-C keeps the stage floor visible.

Front Mezz is only 5 rows deep (A-E) with no balcony above, so every row has clean sightlines — and row B specifically beats row A because a safety railing in front of row A cuts into the stage (one source cites ~35% obstruction for some seats), making B the preferred pick that most guides name by row.

SeatPlan and forum posts flag that the mezzanine overhang starts at row J but begins cutting into the top of the stage from row W back across Left, Center, and Right Orchestra — combined with the Lunt-Fontanne's high unraked stage (floor already hard to see from mid-orchestra), rear orchestra loses both the top and bottom of the picture.

The Lunt-Fontanne has no balcony, so unlike most large Nederlander houses the Rear Mezz has zero overhang — SeatPlan specifically names rows B-C as best because they clear the railing behind the Front Mezz that can obstruct row A, and the section's rake keeps sightlines clean despite being the cheapest seats in the venue.

Multiple guides flag that the Lunt-Fontanne's unusually high, non-raked stage makes rows A-C worse than typical Broadway front rows — Headout and TickPick-linked guides warn sightlines can be obstructed because the stage is raised, and any tall patron in front blocks center-stage action at this proximity.
